data.Documented value: Remembering Ludlow but Forgetting the Columbine: The 1927-1928 Colorado Coal Strike

This dissertation examines the causes, context, and legacies of the 1927-1928 Colorado coal strike in relationship to the history of labor organizing and coalmining in both Colorado and the United States. While historians have written prolifically about the Ludlow Massacre, which took place during the 1913-1914 Colorado coal strike led by the United Mine Workers of America, there has been a curious lack of attention to the Columbine Massacre that occurred not far away within the 1927-1928 Colorado coal strike, led by the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW). This dissertation brings to light an understudied set of significant events and the processes of memory that allowed 1920s era strikes to be forgotten in historical narratives. It thus reveals meaningful and important strands of labor activism in an era often understood to be quiescent.\nA comparative biography of three key participants before, during, and after the 1927-1928 strike—A.S. Embree, the IWW strike leader; Josephine Roche, the owner of the coalmine property where the Columbine Massacre took place; and Powers Hapgood, who came to work for Roche after she signed the 1928 United Mine Workers’ contract—demonstrates the significance of these events to national debates about labor during the period as well as changes and continuities in labor history from the Progressive era to 1930s New Deal labor policies and even through the 1980s.\nReasons why the 1914 Ludlow Massacre has been remembered but the 1927 Columbine Massacre has been forgotten are complex but key to understanding the relationship of these events. Strategic and personal factors helped to shape a narrative that prioritized the well-documented labor militancy and resistance to it during the Progressive era, when Ludlow occurred, over the 1920s and early 1930s, which came to be portrayed as a quiescent era for labor, which, as the biographies show, it was not. Both individuals (such as Roche, Hapgood, and others) and institutions (such as the United Mine Workers and the International Union of Mine, Mill, and Smelter Workers’ Union) needed to put the tumultuous twenties behind them and reinvent themselves in the thirties. In the decades that followed, multiple contexts led both historians and even the original participants to reinforce the forgetting. The history of the Columbine thus reorients scholarly understanding of both labor organizing in the 1920s and the construction of public memory and labor history in Colorado and the United States throughout the 20th century.

paragraphs: ### Colorado construction leader says local expertise paired with national resources creates competitive advantage [[S1|The Business Journals]]

A Colorado construction leader recently highlighted the significant benefits of combining local expertise with national resources in the construction industry. This approach not only enhances the quality of projects but also sets the region apart from others. The leader noted that local knowledge is crucial in understanding the unique challenges and requirements of the local environment, which can significantly impact the design and execution of construction projects. [[S1|The Business Journals]]

National resources, such as advanced technology and materials, can then be leveraged to overcome these challenges. For instance, national research institutions often have access to cutting-edge technology and materials that can be adapted to local conditions. This integration of local expertise with national resources has been shown to create a competitive advantage in the construction industry. The leader emphasized that this approach not only benefits the local economy but also enhances the overall quality of construction projects, leading to better outcomes for both the environment and the community. [[S1|The Business Journals]]

The leader pointed out that this approach is particularly beneficial in regions like the Colorado Plateau, where the environment is diverse and complex. The Colorado Plateau is home to a variety of ecosystems, including deserts, forests, and mountain ranges, each with its own unique challenges. By combining local expertise with national resources, construction leaders can ensure that projects are designed and executed in a way that is sensitive to the local environment, leading to more sustainable and effective outcomes. The leader also highlighted the importance of collaboration between local and national stakeholders. This collaboration is essential for ensuring that projects are not only environmentally sustainable but also economically viable. The leader noted that this approach is not only beneficial for the local community but also for the national economy. By creating a competitive advantage, the region can attract more investment and improve the quality of life for its residents. [[S1|The Business Journals]]

The leader concluded by emphasizing the need for continued research and collaboration between local and national stakeholders. paragraphs: ### Proceedings of the Fourth Biennial Conference of Research on the Colorado Plateau [[S4|OpenAlex research index]] The proceedings of the fourth biennial conference of research on the Colorado Plateau, a series of 13 papers, are a testament to the collaborative efforts of federal, state, and private sector researchers. This series, which has been a cornerstone of scientific information sharing with land managers on the Colorado Plateau, has been the subject of a Preface by the author, reflecting on the pleasure of contributing to this series. The conference, which focuses on providing information to USGS partners, particularly land managers on the Colorado Plateau, has been a significant contributor to the growing pool of scientific data that provides baseline scientific information on the physical, cultural, and biological resources of the Colorado Plateau. [[S4|OpenAlex research index]] The papers of this fourth proceedings contribute to the ongoing efforts to understand and protect the resources of the Colorado Plateau.

These studies have been supported by a broad spectrum of federal, state, and private partners, concerned about the wellbeing of the Plateau's resources. The authors have pursued important lines of work in the four states that comprise the Colorado Plateau biogeographic region, with support from modest funding and a broad base of public and institutional support. [[S4|OpenAlex research index]] As a people, we face the prospect of extensive local and global environmental changes that continue to perturb the physical, cultural, and biological resources on lands of the Colorado Plateau. The research branch for the Department of the Interior, the USGS, is committed to identifying information that can be used by land managers to protect our resources from detrimental change due to modern human influences.

The task of identifying and providing this information has just begun, and the USGS must continue to develop the information necessary to alert managers, leaders, and the public to the importance of their natural surroundings as elements of the basic resources that sustain us, inspire us, and represent our natural biological and environmental heritage. [[S4|OpenAlex research index]] In the fourth section’s fifth paragraph, the first evidence point for Proceedings of the fourth biennial conference of research on the is that as a people, we face the prospect of extensive local and global environmental changes that continue to perturb the physical, cultural, and biological resources on lands of the Colorado Plateau.

sections.heading: INDUSTRIAL POLICY FOR SCALING OFFSITE HOUSING CONSTRUCTION IN THE UNITED
paragraphs: Offsite construction, a set of construction techniques involving offsite prefabrication before onsite building assembly, shows promise as a means of reducing housing construction costs and timelines. Yet the sector accounts for a marginal share of the construction sector in the United States today due to a range of barriers preventing many firms from achieving economic sustainability and efficient project performance. As accelerating construction cost inflation undermines the ability of housing markets to supply enough housing to meet demand, state and local jurisdictions throughout the United States have recently begun pursuing industrial policy efforts to address these barriers and catalyze broader adoption of these techniques. [[S6|Digital Access to Scholarship at Harvard]] This research identifies patterns in these policy initiatives across each stage of their development, progressing from the barriers that motivate them, to their origins, goals, design, and implementation, and concluding with an analysis of Colorado as an advanced case study with sufficient data to permit tentative policy evaluation.

This thesis makes contributions across each stage of the policy cycle. It elaborates on previously understudied barriers to offsite construction and argues that the barriers to the offsite construction form an interconnected system with important policy implications. These include that policy must be mindful of unintended consequences, comprehensive across the many domains of the housing ecosystem in which these barriers exist, and address the vicious cycle between the industry’s reputation and its inability to achieve scale. [[S6|Digital Access to Scholarship at Harvard]] Regarding the policy initiatives themselves, it identifies five broad categories of policy instruments – demand aggregation, regulatory reform, factory subsidies, workforce development, and knowledge diffusion – and identifies three key challenges that have emerged in several policy efforts: achieving regional coordination, sustaining momentum, and opposition from building trades unions.

Finally, it finds that firms supported through Colorado’s policy efforts have yielded cost savings and housing unit production below initial expectations. Though robust causal attribution was prevented by a lack of data, it argues that insufficiently comprehensive regulatory reform and demand aggregation provide significant explanation for these outcomes. [[S6|Digital Access to Scholarship at Harvard]] Offsite construction, a method of prefabricating housing components offsite before assembly on-site, holds promise as a way to reduce construction costs and timelines. However, the sector currently only accounts for a small share of the construction industry due to various barriers that prevent firms from achieving economic sustainability and efficient project performance.

The partnership with CEAS, a leading institution known for its rigorous academic standards and practical engineering education, will provide students with a robust foundation in both fields. [[S1|University of Colorado Boulder]] The program will be designed to meet the needs of the construction industry, which is constantly evolving. Students will learn not only about the technical aspects of construction but also about the business aspects that are crucial for project management and profitability. This dual focus is expected to equip graduates with the skills necessary to succeed in a diverse range of construction roles.

[[S1|University of Colorado Boulder]] The partnership with CEAS is particularly significant for the region, as it brings together the local expertise of Leeds with the national resources of CEAS. This collaboration is expected to attract students from across the state and beyond, contributing to the growth and development of the local construction industry. [[S1|University of Colorado Boulder]] The program will be open to students interested in pursuing a career in construction, engineering, or related fields. The curriculum will be designed to be both academically rigorous and industry-relevant, ensuring that students are well-prepared for the challenges they will face in their future careers.

[[S1|University of Colorado Boulder]] While the program is still in the planning stages, Leeds and CEAS are optimistic about the potential impact it will have on the local construction industry and the region as a whole.
